# Ratana Sutta (Kp 6 (PTS Kp 6))

**ID:** Kp 6 (PTS Kp 6)
**Section:** Khuddakapāṭha (kp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Ratana Sutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Gems
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/kp6
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0501m.mul5.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Ratana Sutta* ("Gems" or "Discourse on the Precious", also translated as "The Jewel Discourse") is the sixth text of the *Khuddakapāṭha* (Kp 6) and is duplicated in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 2.1) [SuttaCentral; Rahula 1978; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Anālayo 2018]. Composed largely in verse, the discourse proclaims the supreme treasures and virtues inherent in the Triple Gem—the Buddha, Dhamma, and Sangha—with seven stanzas specifically detailing the holy qualities of the disciples of the Sangha, such as the "Eight Persons" and "Four Pairs" [SuttaCentral; Rahula 1978; Anālayo 2018]. The text opens by addressing whatever spirits or non-human beings are assembled on earth or in the sky, summoning them to cultivate benevolence towards humans [Gombrich 1991].

The discourse is one of the most prominent *paritta* (protective) recitations in the Theravāda tradition, forming a foundational triad in the *Catubhānavāra* alongside the *Maṅgala Sutta* and the *Mettā Sutta* [Gombrich 1991; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Anālayo 2018]. Both the *Milindapañha* and the *Dīghanikāya* commentary celebrate it as a premier protective chant against calamities and evil spirits [Rahula 1956; Jetjiravat]. According to the commentarial narrative, it was first recited by Ānanda, who sprinkled consecrated water from the Buddha's bowl throughout Vesālī to banish a plague from the city of the Licchavis [Deeg; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. Commentaries also record an ancient divergence of opinion regarding whether the entire discourse was uttered by the Buddha or only the first five verses [Adikaram 1946]. In Sri Lankan history, King Sena II had the sutta engraved upon a gold plate as an object of veneration [Gombrich 1991].

While absent from the Chinese Āgamas [Buswell & Lopez 2014], the sutta has significant non-Pali parallels. Full Sanskrit parallels appear in the *Mahāvastu* (*Svastyayanagāthā* / arrival in Vesālī) [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Lamotte 1988], and the complete text is embedded within the Sanskrit *Mahāsāhasrapramardanī* and its Tibetan translations [DharmaNexus; Holz]. DharmaNexus matches also reveal extensive internal Pali reuse in the *Suttanipāta* (§0.1–19.1) and substantial quotation across canonical and commentarial texts such as the *Kathāvatthu* and *Paramatthajotikā* [DharmaNexus].

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral (suttacentral.net) — Basic metadata, blurb, English title, translation count, and parallel citations (Snp 2.1, Mahāvastu).
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus match data — Computed text-reuse alignments across Pali, Sanskrit (Mahāvastu, Mahāsāhasrapramardanī), and Tibetan texts.
- [Gombrich 1991] Richard F. Gombrich, Buddhist Precept and Practice: Traditional Buddhism in the Rural Highlands of Ceylon (1991) — Notes its place in the Catubhānavāra, its opening address to assembled spirits, and King Sena II's golden plate inscription.
- [Deeg] Max Deeg, Legend and Cult: Contributions to the History of Indian Buddhist Stūpas (Part Two) — Mentions the Khuddakapāṭha commentary (Vesālīvatthu) and the Licchavi legend.
- [Jetjiravat] P. Jetjiravat, Direct Causal Link Between Illness and Kamma: A Buddhist Perspective — Cites the sutta as a paritta recited for protection.
- [Adikaram 1946] E. W. Adikaram, Early History of Buddhism in Ceylon (1946) — Reports commentarial debate on whether the Buddha spoke the whole sutta or only the first five verses.
- [Rahula 1956] Walpola Rahula, History of Buddhism in Ceylon: Anuradhapura Period (1956) — Cites Milindapañha and Dīgha commentary ranking the text among top parittas.
- [Lamotte 1988] Étienne Lamotte, History of Indian Buddhism (1988) — Notes the correspondence of the Khuddakapāṭha's Ratanasutta with the Mahāvastu.
- [Holz] Holz, The Bhadrakarātrī-sūtra: Apotropaic Scriptures in Early Indian Buddhism — Identifies the inclusion of the complete Ratana Sutta in the Sanskrit Mahāsāhasrapramardana-sūtra.
- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. & Donald S. Lopez Jr., The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Details apotropaic role, English title translation, absence in Chinese Āgamas, and the story of Ānanda sprinkling water in Vesālī.
- [Anālayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Rebirth in Early Buddhism & Current Research (2018) — Discusses oral chanting, memorization, and appearance in both Khuddakapāṭha and Sutta-nipāta.
- [Rahula 1978] Walpola Rahula, Zen and the Taming of the Bull (1978) — Discusses the seven verses eulogizing the Sangha, the Eight Persons, and the Four Pairs.
